articles.title: What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Prospect of partial return to Budapest by Central European University suggests confidence in Hungary’s future
A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to expanding its presence in Budapest, in a mark of confidence in the country’s democratic future.
Carsten Q Schneider, the interim president and rector of Central European University (CEU), said it was interested in increasing its programmes in Budapest, as long as this did not damage the student experience.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: University hounded out of Hungary by Orbán reaches out to new government

articles.author: Henry Belot
articles.description:
Sydney and Melbourne airports say flights were affected by now-lifted ban on departures in US

US flight outage – live updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Some US-bound flights from Sydney airport were grounded or delayed on Saturday after American authorities halted departures and delayed landings at all US airports.
Flights from Melbourne airport were also affected, with travel for passengers expected to depart for Los Angeles shortly after 10am being delayed by almost three hours.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US-bound flights out of Australia delayed after telecommunications outage grounded American planes

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell and Taz Ali
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed. Follow our latest coverage here.

US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop affecting all air travel

Chaos at US airports as flight stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

In other tech-related news, the Microsoft outage is still going. The longest in the company’s history. My colleagues are covering the latest and how it’s affecting millions and pretty much every industry …
As I noted earlier, the calls for Howard Lutnick to appear before lawmakers on Capitol Hill have been answered.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US flight outage: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop; Trump officials suggest new tech overwhelmed old equipment – as it happened

articles.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas and Lucy Campbell in New Orleans
articles.description:
No passengers or crew killed or critically hurt after tanker collides with river cruise ship on Mississippi, officials say
In what the city’s mayor declared a “miracle on the Mississippi”, all passengers were accounted for – with none killed or critically hurt – after a tanker collided with a river cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon.
Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals after the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck American Cruise Lines’s American Heritage at about 12.30pm – but none of their injuries were considered critical, New Orleans’s mayor, Helena Moreno, said at a news conference.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: All passengers and crew accounted for after New Orleans boat crash in ‘miracle on the Mississippi’

articles.author: Edward Helmore in New York
articles.description:
Travelers and crew feeling ‘pissed’ or ‘lucky’ depending on level of upset amid nationwide ground stop

Airport chaos continues after FAA lifts ground stop – live updates

The US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw airports and travel plans into chaos across the country, as passengers on planes and in airport terminals were suddenly thrust into limbo.
At New York’s John F Kennedy airport, passengers found their travel plans abruptly cancelled – some even after they’d boarded.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It’s frustrating’: chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt

articles.author: Abené Clayton
articles.description:
Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said the airspace was now open and the problem had been identified

Airport chaos continues after FAA lifts ground stop – live updates

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop that was declared Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware, and throwing airports into sudden chaos.
The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website. “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop affecting all air travel

articles.author: Penry Buckley
articles.description:
The former coalminer’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’ sparked wide criticism, but his party has shown no signs of dumping him

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation’s lead upper house candidate, Stuart Bonds, launches into a speech against “mass” migration.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas
SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short.
Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse

articles.author: Henry Belot and Guardian staff
articles.description:
Experts say outage exposes ‘Australia’s reliance on foreign technology’ as software giant says services being restored

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.
The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global disruption that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia

articles.author: AFP
articles.description:
Statement is rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis
Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.
Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab minority

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure at Suffolk site affected, says US military 
The US Air Force has said it responded to “suspected unauthorised drone activity” on Friday night at an RAF airbase in the east of England.
No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, the air force said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US Air Force responds to suspected drone activity at RAF Lakenheath

articles.author: AFP
articles.description:
Anti-corruption agency carried out searches as part of investigation into Orbán-era minister accused of taking bribes
Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán’s cabinet.
Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hungary seizes $19.5m in cash found buried in forests amid graft inquiry

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to bring shoppers back
The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?
Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Move deals blow to government’s plans to release thousands of prisoners early to tackle prison overcrowding
The government’s plans to release thousands of prisoners early were dealt a blow on Friday after probation officers across England and Wales voted to strike over pay and excessive workloads.
Members of the union, Napo, backed overtime restrictions and other forms of action short of a strike, which is likely to start on 23 November. Plans are being made for strike action to follow at a later stage.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Probation officers in England and Wales vote to strike over pay and workloads

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Dublin
articles.description:
Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security
The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns

articles.author: Shrai Popat in Washington, Jonathan Yerushalmy, Mark Sweney and agencies
articles.description:
US commerce secretary faces sack as questions emerge over senior Trump officials’ knowledge of alleged Chinese spy’s ties to Jensen Huang

US politics – live updates

The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, is facing growing pressure over his apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal as other Trump administration officials publicly raise questions over his decisions.
Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nvidia scandal: US treasury chief blames Lutnick’s commerce department over alleged lack of action

articles.author: Caroline Davies
articles.description:
Barrister say law does not adequately recognise power imbalance between young people and much older adults
Allegations against Russell Brand and, separately, David Walliams, which he denies, have led to calls for greater legal protection for 16- and 17-year-olds from sexual exploitation by older adults.
A staggered consent law is one route favoured by campaigners, supported by some Labour MPs. Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, has called for “serious conversations” on the potential for legislative change.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Walliams allegations prompt calls for staggered age of consent at 16 and 17

articles.author: Emma Loffhagen
articles.description:
Parents take action while several independent bookshops say they had already stopped stocking his titles
In Sarah’s house, David Walliams has been a bedtime staple for years. Her children, aged eight, six and four, have dressed up as his characters for World Book Day – they love the over-the-top, unusual names and illustrations.
Now, all the books are going. “I’ll probably take them away and replace them with other authors,” says Sarah, a mother in west London. “Sooner rather than later, so they don’t realise.” If any of her children ask why, she will tell them “that his choices aren’t great and that I think we should be reading other books”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Families clear homes of David Walliams books after sexual offence allegations

articles.author: Mark Sweney, Josh Taylor, Aisha Down, Emma Elsworthy and Lauren Aratani
articles.description:
Tech firm says it is ‘deeply sorry’ for disruption that took services down and has now addressed the underlying issue

What caused the outage and when will it be fixed?

Microsoft outage hits UK hospitals, GPs, schools and police

Tell us: have you been affected by the outage?

Microsoft has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Microsoft outage: company scrambles to fix global issue that took down Outlook and Teams

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Mohammed Alfatih rearrested over alleged plot to target Israelis in Europe while detained for attack on bailiff
A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in Germany for allegedly plotting to murder Jewish people.
Details of the alleged plot can now be reported after Mohammed Alfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, was found guilty on Friday of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his home in Birmingham.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Former Hamas bodyguard convicted of Birmingham knife crime also wanted in Germany

articles.author: Jakub Krupa
articles.description:
This blog is now closed
Hungary’s Péter Magyar is also here, looking very elegant as always…
… but it looks like he took a slight detour on the way back to hotel last night to try and pour a perfect pint of Guinness.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Europe should not walk into Russia’s ‘traps’ on Ukraine talks, EU’s foreign policy chief Kallas says – as it happened

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months.
“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran says it targeted US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike

articles.author: Ariel Bogle
articles.description:
Young people are being found with ‘hard drives full of what can only be described as gore’, one expert says

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.
This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What’s behind Australia’s surge in teen extremism?

articles.author: Ed Walton and Alice Nightingale-Smith for MetDesk
articles.description:
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week 
Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe

articles.author: Sarah Johnson
articles.description:
Political prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran, given prestigious Magnitsky humanitarian award 
A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.
Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran. He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Boxer on death row in Iran vows ‘not to bow before oppression’ after winning rights prize

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Danny Vincent and Nathan Law; produced by Guy Szafman and Brian McNamara; executive producers Sami Kent and Alex Atack
articles.description:
Pro-democracy activist Nathan Law and journalist Danny Vincent on the sentencing of the iconic Hong Kong campaigner Joshua Wong to another 10 years in prison. Send your comments and questions to tif.questions@theguardian.com
He has been leading protests since he was 14. Joshua Wong has been on the cover of Time magazine, the focus of a Netflix documentary and an icon for Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement.
Wong has been leading the fight against a Chinese squeeze on freedoms in Hong Kong for the last 15 years. He will now spend more than 16 years in prison.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Teen prodigy, Netflix star, prisoner: the story of Hong Kong dissident Joshua Wong – podcast

articles.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
articles.description:
Decision disappoints experts hoping for world’s biggest emitter to take global lead on climate crisis 
China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.
The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets
Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two men found guilty of helping Iran try to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists

articles.author: Agencies and Guardian sport
articles.description:
F1 driver urges Israel to let aid into Gaza

Trip involved tour of facilities with aid workers

Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel must allow aid ⁠trucks into Gaza, a day after he visited the Rafah border crossing in Egypt.
Hamilton, a seven-time ⁠world champion, arrived ⁠in ​El Arish on Tuesday, where he was briefed on how aid is prepared and coordinated before it ⁠is sent into Gaza, as he toured the Rafah crossing and the Egyptian Red Crescent’s aid warehouses.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lewis Hamilton says ‘Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling’ after Rafah visit

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies
articles.description:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story

articles.author: Hettie O'Brien
articles.description:
In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang

Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.
Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.
UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.
US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.
Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair

articles.author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
Remains believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians repatriated after being flown back by diplomats 
Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.
The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies

articles.author: Facundo Iglesia in Buenos Aires and agencies
articles.description:
Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody
A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.
Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina

articles.author: Daniel Boffey in Hamburg
articles.description:
Lawyer says Britain wrong to believe in historic doctrine that crown has sovereignty over parts of oceans
Britain should not be permitted to act as a 17th-century colonial power treating the waters around the Falkland Islands as a Dominium maris Britannici, Argentina has told an international tribunal.
Marcelo Kohen, representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked Britain for apparently believing in the historic doctrine that the British crown has sovereignty over expansive parts of the oceans.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Argentinian lawyer mocks UK’s sovereignty claim in Falklands oil case

articles.author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
articles.description:
Tomás Beltrán was shot dead amid gang warfare that has turned Latin American country into one of its most violent
Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.
Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Killing of journalist underscores deteriorating conditions in Ecuador

articles.author: Kate Lamb
articles.description:
Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort
Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.
The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment

articles.author: Associated Press at the Rafah crossing
articles.description:
Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi
articles.description:
Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising
Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a new passport this week.
Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven

articles.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester

articles.author: Rebecca Ratcliffe, Gloria Dickie and Elisângela Mendonça
articles.description:
Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo
The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm

articles.author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies
articles.description:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final years
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’

articles.author: Patrick Greenfield, Elisângela Mendonça and Phoebe Weston and Spoorthy Raman
articles.description:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of  Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.
This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying

articles.author: Edward Helmore in New York
articles.description:
Travelers and crew feeling ‘pissed’ or ‘lucky’ depending on level of upset amid nationwide ground stop

Airport chaos continues after FAA lifts ground stop – live updates

The US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw airports and travel plans into chaos across the country, as passengers on planes and in airport terminals were suddenly thrust into limbo.
At New York’s John F Kennedy airport, passengers found their travel plans abruptly cancelled – some even after they’d boarded.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It’s frustrating’: chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt

articles.author: Abené Clayton
articles.description:
Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said the airspace was now open and the problem had been identified

Airport chaos continues after FAA lifts ground stop – live updates

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop that was declared Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware, and throwing airports into sudden chaos.
The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website. “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop affecting all air travel

articles.author: Chris Stein
articles.description:
Maryland senator’s bid against Chuck Schumer for leadership could decide direction of the Democratic party

US politics live – latest updates

Ever since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Democratic officeholders and voters alike have been divided over whether their leader in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, is up to the task of taking the president on.
That debate intensified on Thursday, when the Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen announced he will challenge Schumer for the post of Democratic Senate leader, which will become one of the most powerful jobs in Washington when the party takes control of Congress’s upper chamber next year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: As Van Hollen wages a challenge, Senate Democrats are torn on whom to elect as their leader

articles.author: Bernie Sanders
articles.description:
This is not a personality contest. This is a debate about the future of the Democratic party
The election for Democratic Senate leader between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen must be understood for what it is.
This is not a personality contest. This is a debate about the future of the Democratic party. It is a debate about whether the Democratic party remains a top-down party dominated by billionaire campaign contributors, inside-the-beltway consultants and 30-second TV ads, or whether we can transform it into a grassroots party of, by and for the working families of our country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What the choice between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen for Senate leader is all about | Bernie Sanders

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
Seven Americans on their hopes for Colom, 43, Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction
Democrat Scott Colom made history this month, becoming Mississippi’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era after defeating incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The 43-year-old’s win also contributed to a Democratic majority of at least 55 seats in the Senate – the party’s largest midterm gains since 1986.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Across racial lines, Americans celebrate Scott Colom’s historic election: ‘The times they are a-changin’

articles.author: Guardian community team
articles.description:
Kai Wright of the Guardian podcast Stateside will speak with author and environmentalist Bill McKibben – and we’d like to hear your questions
Was the climate crisis one of your top political priorities during the midterm elections? We want to hear from you: what do you want political leaders to do about it in 2027?
Democrats will control the House and Senate in the new year, and they have a long list of priorities ahead of them. But it remains to be seen just how much they will focus on one of the most pressing issues of our times: the climate crisis. The UN declared this summer that, despite some progress, it is now “unavoidable” that the globe will heat past the point that scientists say will threaten human health. Despite these terrifying predictions, the US remains absent from global efforts to limit the impacts of the climate crisis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Send us your questions about climate crisis and politics for the next Stateside guest: Bill McKibben

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Aisha Down ; produced by Hana Williams ; senior producer Angus Neale ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
articles.description:
Jensen Huang’s resignation from the AI chipmaker Nvidia has sent shockwaves through the global economy. Huang resigned after reported affairs with an Nvidia executive and a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The fallout is not over yet, with criticism mounting over the apparent lack of action from the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s global technology reporter, Aisha Down
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why the Nvidia scandal is far from over - The Latest

articles.author: Editorial
articles.description:
From Cairo to Moscow to Washington, governments are turning up the pressure on media workers
Lina Attalah is an influential Egyptian journalist. Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October, resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month.
Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Guardian view on press freedom: authoritarians target journalism because it matters | Editorial

articles.author: Brigid Schulte and Haley Swenson
articles.description:
Amid concerns over the influence of the manosphere, our findings show that young men are concerned about caregiving
When young men helped propel Donald Trump into the White House in 2024, the administration doubled down on a brand of toxic masculinity popular in the so-called manosphere.
They touted high testosterone, male supremacy, and a “biblically-based family” where men work and provide, and deferential women stay home to bear children and care for others.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Young men were key to the blue wave. Our research offers a reason why | Brigid Schulte and Haley Swenson

articles.author: Fabiola Cineas
articles.description:
After Tuesday’s election, ‘everyone must have a Wednesday agenda,’ experts say
The bright blue map that emerged on election night in the US was unthinkable two years ago. When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, many Democratic voters curled up in bed and doomscrolled, fatigued and fearful about the direction of the country. Any desire to fight back was dampened by the enormity of the loss.
But the mood gradually shifted over the following two years, culminating in a generational shift on election day: Democrats flipped five governors’ seats and took control of the House and Senate by wide margins. Voters were angry about the rising cost of living, the war in Iran, masked immigration agents in their neighborhoods and datacenters rising in their backyards.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Democrats won big in the US midterms. Now, organizers want them to deliver

articles.author: Claire Finkelstein
articles.description:
The failed move could lead to a more robust effort against the defense secretary in the next Congress. Here’s how it could look
A traffic jam, combined with disorganization on the part of Democrats, enabled House Republicans to scuttle the representative Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.
While recriminations are now flying among Democrats, the fumble may have been a blessing in disguise. Democrats can now refocus the articles against the defense secretary, possibly to better effect.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Democrats fumbled the Hegseth impeachment. That could be a blessing in disguise | Claire Finkelstein

articles.author: Presented by Jonathan Freedland , with Susan Glasser, produced by Danielle Stephens and May Robson
articles.description:
Jonathan Freedland speaks to Susan Glasser of the New Yorker about why Trump’s judgment of high-profile men is questionable
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why the Nvidia cheating scandal is bad for Trump | Politics Weekly America

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with George Chidi ; produced by Angus Neale ; senior producer Leonore Schick ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
articles.description:
Mississippi has elected the Democrat Scott Colom in a historic race in the traditionally deep-red state, making him its first Black senator since shortly after the US civil war. The closely contested race was called more than a week after the US midterms, with Colom running against the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. How did Colom’s grassroots campaign win despite limited early backing from national Democrats? Lucy Hough speaks to politics and democracy reporter George Chidi
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mississippi makes history with Democrat Scott Colom’s Senate win - The Latest

articles.author: Abené Clayton
articles.description:
Some advocates say it no longer makes sense for their movement to be so intertwined with the Republican party
After the Democrats’ huge wins in the US midterm elections last week, gun rights advocates are updating their strategies in an attempt to cross the aisle and find allies on the left.
While most of the biggest and most visible gun rights groups, such as the National Rifle Association (NRA), are already signaling that they will challenge any gun safety legislation brought by the new Democratic Congress, others say it no longer makes sense for their movement to be so deeply intertwined with the Republican party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Gun rights groups plot new ties with ‘gun owners who vote Democrat’ after midterms verdict

articles.author: Alyssa Mercante
articles.description:
Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House
In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade, it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia.
After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda

articles.author: Byard Duncan, Sophie Sullivan and Michael Hudson
articles.description:
Complaints about banks and other financial players keep rising as Trump officials squelch enforcement actions at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau

 This story was supported and co-published by the journalism 
non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project

 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Screwed twice’: The CFPB says it’s looking out for consumers. Its own data tells a different story

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright , produced by Anabel Bacon and Tiara Chiaramonte , engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Jonathan Menjivar
articles.description:
Pete Hegseth has managed to dodge an impeachment trial, for the second time. And Republicans have avoided — for now — a major public accounting of the damage done at the Pentagon during Hegseth’s tenure. Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment detail charges that are likely to return when Democrats take the majority next year. Kai Wright speaks with Guardian senior political enterprise reporter Aram Roston about how people inside the military have reacted to the impeachment and to Hegseth’s tenure, from the boat strikes in the Caribbean to the massive loss of experienced leadership and a dramatic depletion of munitions in Iran. Roston, who has covered the Pentagon across several administrations, describes a Pentagon shaken up in ways he’s never before seen.

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pete Hegseth’s wake of destruction at the Pentagon – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure at Suffolk site affected, says US military 
The US Air Force has said it responded to “suspected unauthorised drone activity” on Friday night at an RAF airbase in the east of England.
No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, the air force said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US Air Force responds to suspected drone activity at RAF Lakenheath

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to bring shoppers back
The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?
Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Move deals blow to government’s plans to release thousands of prisoners early to tackle prison overcrowding
The government’s plans to release thousands of prisoners early were dealt a blow on Friday after probation officers across England and Wales voted to strike over pay and excessive workloads.
Members of the union, Napo, backed overtime restrictions and other forms of action short of a strike, which is likely to start on 23 November. Plans are being made for strike action to follow at a later stage.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Probation officers in England and Wales vote to strike over pay and workloads

articles.author: Vikram Dodd and Hannah Al-Othman
articles.description:
Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents have had to find a workaround for Microsoft packages
Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents across the UK have been hit by the global Microsoft outage. Here’s how the disruption to email and other IT facilities has affected key services.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Microsoft outage has affected key public services in the UK

articles.author: Caroline Davies
articles.description:
Barrister say law does not adequately recognise power imbalance between young people and much older adults
Allegations against Russell Brand and, separately, David Walliams, which he denies, have led to calls for greater legal protection for 16- and 17-year-olds from sexual exploitation by older adults.
A staggered consent law is one route favoured by campaigners, supported by some Labour MPs. Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, has called for “serious conversations” on the potential for legislative change.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Walliams allegations prompt calls for staggered age of consent at 16 and 17

articles.author: Emma Loffhagen
articles.description:
Parents take action while several independent bookshops say they had already stopped stocking his titles
In Sarah’s house, David Walliams has been a bedtime staple for years. Her children, aged eight, six and four, have dressed up as his characters for World Book Day – they love the over-the-top, unusual names and illustrations.
Now, all the books are going. “I’ll probably take them away and replace them with other authors,” says Sarah, a mother in west London. “Sooner rather than later, so they don’t realise.” If any of her children ask why, she will tell them “that his choices aren’t great and that I think we should be reading other books”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Families clear homes of David Walliams books after sexual offence allegations

articles.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
articles.description:
Met police say allegations are separate from those made by multiple women in Guardian and ITV investigation
The Metropolitan police have launched a criminal investigation into David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences.
Walliams, 55, was accused in reports by ITV and the Guardian this week of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex. He has denied any wrongdoing, being a sexual predator or breaking the law.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police launch investigation into David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences

articles.author: Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot
articles.description:
No 10 sources say PM wants party to refocus on Tories as electoral threat after prioritising Reform and Greens
Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “rearm” to fight the Conservatives at the next election amid concern inside government that they must take the prospect of a Kemi Badenoch-led recovery seriously.
Downing Street sources said the prime minister wanted Labour headquarters to refocus on the Tories as an electoral threat after more than two years of prioritising Nigel Farage’s Reform and, on their left flank, the Greens.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Andy Burnham urges Labour to ‘rearm’ for Kemi Badenoch comeback

articles.author: Aletha Adu political correspondent
articles.description:
Anneliese Midgley surprises colleagues after Burnham said whips’ office should not be ‘something to be feared’
If Andy Burnham has been accused of being a people pleaser by his critics, the same most certainly cannot be said of his chief whip.
“I’m not going to take any shit and I don’t fuck about,” said Anneliese Midgley, the Labour government’s newest head of party discipline, shedding some light on her direct approach to keeping MPs in line.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labour chief whip tells Vogue she takes tough approach to keeping MPs in line

articles.author: Ben Quinn, Aisha Down, Andrew Gregory and Jamie Grierson
articles.description:
NHS suffering ‘serious’ and widespread disruption, while people are told of possible delays in receiving prescriptions
Vital UK services have been hit by a global Microsoft outage that left hospital staff resorting to paper records and fuelled concerns about an over-reliance on a small number of tech companies.
A day of widespread disruption sent some sectors back to the 1990s, with court staff looking for fax machines and rail travellers being warned they might not be able to rely on digital tickets.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Microsoft outage hits hospitals, GPs, schools and police across UK

articles.author: Daniel Boffey Chief reporter
articles.description:
It has been suggested that women with stories to tell felt silenced after signing non-disclosure agreements
The UK’s minister for women has suggested that the government has not gone far enough in tackling the abusive use of non-disclosure agreements.
Bridget Phillipson was commenting in the context of the allegations of improper behaviour by David Walliams – which he denies – and the conviction of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault. In both cases, it has been suggested that women with stories to tell felt silenced after signing an NDA.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: After Walliams and Brand, how could the UK government tackle NDAs?

articles.author: Mark Sweney, Josh Taylor, Aisha Down, Emma Elsworthy and Lauren Aratani
articles.description:
Tech firm says it is ‘deeply sorry’ for disruption that took services down and has now addressed the underlying issue

What caused the outage and when will it be fixed?

Microsoft outage hits UK hospitals, GPs, schools and police

Tell us: have you been affected by the outage?

Microsoft has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Microsoft outage: company scrambles to fix global issue that took down Outlook and Teams

articles.author: Josh Taylor, Aisha Down and Mark Sweney
articles.description:
Problem affects businesses, government agencies and even tech firm’s own employees

Microsoft scrambles to fix global outage affecting Teams and Outlook

Microsoft outage – live updates

Tell us: have you been affected by the Microsoft outage?

Millions of people were unable to access their emails, Teams chats or meetings on Thursday night and Friday after a Microsoft 365 outage brought down services across the globe.
The outage has lasted for more than 21 hours, with meaningful signs of recovery visible beginning shortly before midday GMT on Friday. It affected businesses, government agencies and even Microsoft employees all over the world. Those reporting issues have included the US House of Representatives, an Australian spy agency, airlines in India, European government agencies, and police services, ambulances and hospitals in the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A global Microsoft 365 outage has hit millions – what happened and when will it be fixed?

articles.author: Jasper Jolly
articles.description:
JLR chief executive calls for EU and Britain to join forces amid competition from Chinese electric carmakers
Jaguar Land Rover has reported a £451m quarterly loss as it counts the cost of cutting 4,000 jobs, while its chief executive has called for the EU and Britain to work together in the face of competition from China.
Britain’s largest automotive employer reported revenues rising to £5.9bn between July and September, but it recorded £530m in costs from the job cuts announced near the end of that period amid tough trading conditions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jaguar Land Rover reports £451m quarterly loss after cutting 4,000 jobs

articles.author: Joanna Partridge
articles.description:
Signing of agreement to smooth movement of food, plants and animals next week will not recoup huge sums firms were forced to spend
The removal of border checks and paperwork on plant imports will “dissolve” £60m of annual costs for the horticulture industry when the UK and EU’s new post-Brexit deal comes in, the environment secretary has said.
Before the UK-EU summit on 20 November, Angela Eagle said she hoped paperwork headaches for importers would “disappear” after the changes, although the move would not help businesses recoup the large sums they spent to deal with border controls.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK-EU deal will ‘dissolve’ £60m a year of costs for plant trade, says Angela Eagle

articles.author: Tom Ambrose (now) and Taz Ali (earlier)
articles.description:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally has said “people are seeking meaning, connection and hope in a turbulent world” as new statistics reveal Church of England attendances have grown for the fifth year in a row.
The number of regular attenders to C of E services grew to 1.03m in 2025, a 1.5% increase on the previous year.
Whether at morning prayer, a Sunday service, Evensong, a youth hub, a parent and toddler group - or any of the countless ways that the Church of England serves our communities in every parish - it is clear that people are seeking meaning, connection and hope in a turbulent world.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Row breaks out between Tories and Reform at Piddington news conference – as it happened

articles.author: Matthew Pearce and Pippa Neill
articles.description:
Exclusive: Government in ‘private meetings’ about removing cost cap protections under Aarhus convention
The government is considering stripping back legal protections that limit the costs community groups face when challenging planning decisions that threaten nature.
The Aarhus convention, an environmental treaty that was signed into law by the UK in 2005, guarantees the legal right to participate in democratic processes on environmental matters – such as sewage pollution, new roads or datacentre developments.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Right to make green challenges to planning decisions under threat, say UK lawyers

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Chris Philp and Zia Yusuf trade barbs in Oxfordshire village planning legal action to block conversion of military base
Senior Tory and Reform politicians have clashed over immigration policy in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington after the government approved plans to convert a defence site into accommodation for asylum seekers.
Zia Yusuf and Chris Philp raised their voices and spoke over each other in front of TV cameras and local people for more than three minutes. Yusuf urged his fellow home affairs spokesperson to apologise for his record as a minister. Philp said they should instead “stand in solidarity with residents” and Yusuf should “read the room”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tories and Reform clash over migration as asylum centre is approved

articles.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
articles.description:
Judge imposes three-year treatment order on Donaldson for aiding and abetting sexual offences by her husband, Jeffrey
Jeffrey Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, has been placed on the sex offender register for five years for aiding and abetting sexual offences by her disgraced husband.
Eleanor Donaldson appeared via remote link at Newry crown court to hear the order on Friday one month after her husband, the former Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, was convicted of abusing two women when they were children.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eleanor Donaldson, wife of former DUP leader, placed on sex offender register

articles.author: Anna Isaac and Ben Quinn
articles.description:
Exclusive: Sources reveal party is covering costs – raising fresh questions about leader’s explanation for billionaire’s gift
Nigel Farage’s personal security has been paid for out of Reform UK’s central funds despite his claim that these expenses would be covered by an undisclosed gift of £5m from a billionaire donor, sources have told the Guardian.
The Reform leader has had the central party pay for a team and two cars ever since a reduction in the security provided by the taxpayer after a review in 2025.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nigel Farage’s security paid for by Reform UK despite claim over £5m gift

articles.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Siberian rubythroat was thousands of miles off course from its route to winter in south or south-east Asia
A bird that flies south from its breeding grounds in Siberia to winter in south and south-east Asia has been found thousands of miles off course in Cumbria. Regrettably, it was found by a cat.
Chris Hind, Cumbria’s county recorder for birds, said it was “extraordinary” that a Siberian rubythroat was found on his patch, albeit dead. There have been only 17 recorded instances of the bird in the UK, 15 of those in the northern Scottish isles.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Incredibly unusual’ bird migrating from Siberia found in Cumbria – killed by cat

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
articles.description:
Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’
The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis.
Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK’s biggest insurer hit by rise in subsidence claims after record hot summer

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Government considers further curbs on non-disclosure agreements after Guardian investigation of TV personality
Ministers are looking at ways to change the law quickly to expand protections that stop non-disclosure agreements being used to cover up harassment or discrimination in the wake of the allegations about David Walliams.
This could involve extending measures that mean an NDA cannot be used this way to silence an employee so that it also applies to others, such as freelancers or volunteers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK ministers look at quick ways to limit NDAs after Walliams allegations

articles.author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
articles.description:
‘I must now listen to my body and my doctors’, says Taylor, who was one of the earliest members of the new wave hit-makers
The drummer for Duran Duran, Roger Taylor, is to step down from the band due to worsening tinnitus.
In a statement, Taylor said: “This is one of the hardest decisions I’ve ever had to make. Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I’ll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they’ve shown us over the years. But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse, and I’ve reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor leaves band due to tinnitus

articles.author: Presented by Kiran Stacey and Jessica Elgot, produced by Saskia Collette, music by Axel Kacoutié; executive producer Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
This week, Kemi Badenoch roasted the prime minister at PMQs with gag after gag. But while the leader of the opposition looks feisty, are some Labour MPs also beginning to wonder if Andy Burnham has the substance to back his policy agenda?
Plus, with the social media ban looking likely to include companies such as Vinted, deputy political editor Jessica Elgot explains the government’s thinking
Read Kiran’s article on jitters about Burnham’s 10-year plan here
Read Jessica’s article on the social media ban here
Send any questions for Pippa and Kiran to politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com
Watch Politics Weekly on our YouTube channel here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Are cracks showing in the Burnham project? – podcast

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Just 28% of 18- and 19-year-olds have received their first dose in one-off campaign, UKHSA says
The clock is ticking for young people in the UK to receive vaccinations to protect against meningitis B, experts have said, as figures reveal fewer than one in three eligible in a one-off campaign have received their first dose.
Earlier this year, an unprecedented outbreak of meningitis B in Kent and clusters of cases in Dorset and Berkshire caused three deaths, as well as lifelong health consequences among some of those who survived.

articles.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
articles.description:
Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.
Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Unprecedented view of cosmos provided by Euclid mission throws up many more cases of gravitational lensing
A mission to create the largest ever 3D map of the universe has revealed more than 900m galaxies in its first major data release together with about 15,000 potential cases of a phenomenon that could help unlock the secrets of the “dark universe”.
Launched in July 2023, the European Space Agency’s Euclid mission promised to create the largest cosmic map ever made, encompassing a third of the sky and more than 10bn years of cosmic history.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: European survey reveals 900m galaxies – and possibly secrets of ‘dark universe’

articles.author: Jasper Jolly
articles.description:
Regulator to hasten review over concerns that firms are ‘undermining’ rules to make large payments to bosses

Business live – latest updates

The water company bonus ban is set to be tightened after the regulator accused the industry of a risk of “damaging public trust” with large payments to bosses that appeared to get around the rules.
Anglian Water was singled out for particular criticism over “retention payments” worth up to £800,000 for its chief executive, Mark Thurston, despite the bonus ban. Anglian will face increased monitoring of its governance arrangements because of the controversial payments.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Water industry bonus ban to be tightened as Ofwat warns of ‘damage to public trust’

articles.author: Severin Carrell Scotland editor
articles.description:
Once thought to have been looted by Scottish tribes, the gilded limb is the centrepiece of a new exhibition on Roman Scotland in Edinburgh
A large bronze leg found in a bog in rural Scotland more than 200 years ago and then hidden away in a duke’s storeroom is helping to rewrite the history of the Roman empire.
Antiquarians argued that the so-called Milsington leg had been looted, perhaps from York, hacked off by marauding Scottish tribes and carried north over Hadrian’s Wall. “We cannot visualise the conditions which would have led to its erection anywhere north of the Great Wall,” said one scholar, James Curle, in 1932.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bronze leg found in Scottish bog sheds new light on Roman occupation

Broadcaster plans to make £30m in ‘temporary’ savings before inquiry into takeover by Sky
ITV plans to slash its programming budget as new figures showed that spend on the production of films and prestige TV shows in the UK was down more than £2bn over the last year.
The broadcaster plans to make £30m in “temporary” savings, including £25m in content and £5m elsewhere in the business.

articles.title: ITV to cut show budgets as UK TV and film production spend drops by more than £2bn

articles.author: Denis Campbell and Tobi Thomas

Action on 25 and 26 November suspended to allow for formal negotations with the government
Senior hospital doctors in England have called off the 48-hour strike they intended to hold later this month after the health secretary agreed to negotiations about their grievances.
NHS chiefs, who were worried about how hospitals would cope during the action, welcomed the decision by consultants to “pause” their walkout, which was scheduled for 25 and 26 November.

articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.description:
This blog is now closed
Here are some more comments on the report for the Casey commission released today looking at how social care is run in England. (See 9.56am.)
This is from Natasha Curry, deputy director of research at the Nuffield Trust and one of the report’s authors.
Compared to the other countries we looked at, the governance of England’s social care system is confused and complex. Overlapping and unclear roles leave dangerous uncertainty around who is responsible for important decisions, contributing to the inertia around reform England has struggled with for decades. The serious consequences of this were laid bare during the Covid pandemic.
The system for governing adult social care in England has evolved haphazardly and with little clear planning. That has been exacerbated by successive governments ducking politically unpalatable decisions for decades. That has scattered responsibility for the sector across and outside government in a way that few would design from scratch.
This report makes for sober reading of how adult social care and those who rely on it have been systematically failed. The fragmentation we see today is what happens when there is a total absence of political leadership to ensure the sector is well-funded and provides equitable access to care.

Exclusive: Cutting 2030 goal would be a ‘step backwards’, say MPs, as ministers clash over proposed reductions 
Labour MPs are urging the government not to weaken its electric vehicle targets as divided cabinet ministers prepare for a crunch meeting on Thursday to thrash out a compromise.
Members of the climate and nature crisis caucus (CNCC) say ministers must not water down a legal requirement for carmakers to ensure that 80% of the vehicles they sell in 2030 are electric, saying doing so would be a backward step and “shortsighted”.

Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say
An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.
Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed.

Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of ‘cacophony’ of noise causing sleep deprivation and depression
When Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home.
“It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester. Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”.

A crisis in post-adoption support in England is making some adoptive parents feel they have nowhere to turn when things go wrong. Jessica Murray reports
In 2013, Victoria adopted two young children, a brother and a sister. At first everything seemed to be going well. But as he grew older, her son’s behaviour became increasingly extreme.
‘I was not in any way, shape or form prepared for the significant level of trauma that the two children that I adopted were dealing with,’ she told Helen Pidd.

Scheme in Derry aims to sow confidence by getting people with learning and physical disabilities into wrestling
The music thumped, the lights blazed and from the ring the announcer did a countdown. “Who is ready to rumble?” he roared. The bellows and cheers indicated that the crowd at St Columb’s Hall in Derry on Saturday night was more than ready for the Foyle Rumble, and so began a wrestling extravaganza of heroes and villains in leotards, masks and kneepads.
The blend of athleticism and scripted storytelling would have been familiar to fans of WrestleMania, but this Northern Irish version came with a twist: many of the performers have learning or physical disabilities, and the characters they play in the ring do not quite stay in the ring.

“The only time we’re regarded as human beings is when they need a lot of hands onboard, like during Covid. But after that, we’re tossed away like we’re some rubbish,” Aneisha Williams says.

The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.

The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country
Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people.
Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. That includes Cornell University, Penn State University, Elgin Community College, Emory University, Binghamton University, Kent State University and the University of Wisconsin’s Madison, Milwaukee and Oshkosh branches. Last week, the University of Buffalo announced an indefinite pause on its plans for a 60-day pilot program.
